---
title: "Testing and Operations"
---


This appendix describes the machinery that decides whether a change is real. It is
an appendix because it is about process rather than architecture — but it is the
part that makes everything in the other chapters trustworthy.

## The test suite {#sec-tests-suite}

Tests live in `tests/`, one module per subsystem, written with `unittest`-style
assertions and run under pytest with asyncio in automatic mode
(`pyproject.toml`). There are 36 modules. The distribution says what the project
actually worries about:

| Area | Representative modules |
|------|-------------------------|
| Channels | `test_backend_channel.py`, `test_dashboard_channel.py`, `test_email_channel.py`, `test_dashboard_cli.py` |
| Sessions | `test_session_rotation.py`, `test_sessions_index.py`, `test_archival_flag.py`, `test_history_trimmer.py`, `test_session_concurrency.py`, `test_session_topic_signal.py` |
| Agent behaviour | `test_steer_btw.py`, `test_task_cancel.py`, `test_tool_validation.py`, `test_skills_summary_compact.py`, `test_has_image_content.py` |
| Providers | `test_providers_manager.py`, `test_provider_role_dispatch.py`, `test_provider_cache_usage.py`, `test_provider_streaming_usage.py` |
| Usage ledger | `test_usage_store.py`, `test_usage_recording.py`, `test_usage_footer.py` |
| Operations | `test_cron_service.py`, `test_cron_commands.py`, `test_commands.py`, `test_heartbeat_service.py`, `test_cli_input.py` |

Run them with:

```bash
pytest                       # everything
pytest tests/test_cron_service.py   # one module
ruff check sarathy/          # lint
```

## Test isolation is not optional {#sec-tests-isolation}

The single most important fixture in the suite is an autouse one that redirects
the usage store to a per-test temporary database and resets the module-level
singleton around every test. Without it, any test that runs the agent loop would
append rows to the real telemetry ledger.

The store defends itself a second time: if it detects it is running under a test
runner and no explicit path was provided, it diverts to a temporary database. Two
independent nets exist because the cost of getting this wrong — a test suite that
quietly corrupts production data — is much higher than the cost of the redundancy.

The same principle appears in the product: the backend channel's jobs-database
access is read-only, so a bug there cannot corrupt the ledger it reads.

## What a regression test looks like here {#sec-tests-regression}

Two examples, because they show what "verify before close" produces.

**Stale-cache rotation.** The dashboard new-chat regression (`9d9747c`) did not
stop at "it archives now". It added a test for the specific shape of the bug: a
session that is *live in the cache* with messages since the last save, rotated
through the new-chat path, and asserted that the archive contains the cached
messages rather than the on-disk snapshot.

**Contract tests for an external interface.** The backend channel tests build a
real database with a real events table, construct the channel against it, and
exercise the HTTP endpoint end to end — including the authorisation path, the
envelope validation path, the high-watermark behaviour on first run, and the
event-type filter. The envelope validation is a pure function, so it is tested
directly as well.

## Verify before close {#sec-tests-verify}

The rule, stated once and applied everywhere:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-verify-loop
%%| fig-cap: "Verify before close. The loop only ends when the artifact has been looked at, and any fix discovered during verification sends you back through the tests."
flowchart LR
  CODE["Write the change<br/>tests land with it"] --> T1["1 · Re-run the tests"]
  T1 -->|fail| CODE
  T1 -->|green| LIVE["2 · Exercise the live thing<br/>call it, load it, send it"]
  LIVE --> INSPECT["3 · Inspect the artifact"]
  INSPECT -->|fix needed| CODE
  INSPECT -->|looks right| T2["4 · Re-run the tests again"]
  T2 --> CLOSE["Close and log"]
  LIVE -.->|"flaky?"| FLAKE["Record as a defect.<br/>Retry until green is silence."]
  style INSPECT fill:#eaf3ec,stroke:#5f8a6d
  style FLAKE fill:#f7f0e6,stroke:#b08a3e
```

1. **Re-run the tests.** Green from an earlier run is not evidence.
2. **Exercise the live thing.** Call the endpoint. Load the page. Send the message.
3. **Inspect the artifact.** Read the output that will be handed over; do not
   infer it from the code that produced it.
4. **Re-run the tests again** if you changed anything while verifying.

And the corollary: **a flaky test is a defect, not bad luck.** A suite that has to
be re-run to be believed is not green, it is noisy. Re-run once to confirm;
if it fails again, record it as a defect and fix the ordering or the shared state.
Retrying until it passes converts a real signal into silence.

## Change taxonomy and the action each requires {#sec-ops-matrix}

| Change kind | Examples | Verification | Runtime action |
|-------------|----------|--------------|----------------|
| Pure logic | session rotation policy, marker parsing, tool validation | unit tests | none |
| Behavioural | concurrency, routing, session archival stamping | unit tests covering the specific bug shape | none |
| Interface contract | backend envelope validation, config schema | contract tests against the real consumer shape | none |
| Configuration | model, provider, temperature, reasoning effort | read back the persisted config | none — hot-reloaded on next turn |
| Skill content | editing a `SKILL.md` | the file watcher log line | none — reloaded in place |
| Scheduler state | editing the cron job file | list the jobs after the change | **restart required** |
| Gateway source | anything under `sarathy/` | full suite plus lint | **redeploy script, then restart** |

The last two rows are the ones people get wrong, and they are wrong in opposite
directions: editing scheduler state and waiting for it to take effect, and
restarting the gateway for a configuration change that hot-reloads. The
distinguishing question is simple: *does any long-lived process hold this in
memory?* If yes, the change needs a restart. If no, it does not.

## Restart procedure {#sec-ops-restart}

Configuration-only:

```
sarathy gateway restart
sarathy gateway status
sarathy gateway logs --follow
```

Source: run the redeploy script. It reinstalls the package, writes a
restart-request flag naming where the confirmation should go, restarts the daemon
through its own CLI, and lets the new process consume the flag and send a boot
notification reporting the version and provider status.

The flag is the important part of the design: a restart is asynchronous from the
operator's point of view, so the request is written to disk *before* the restart
happens. That turns a silent restart into an observable one.

**Never kill the daemon by process-name pattern.** A recorded incident: the pattern
matched the shell command that was running the kill, so the session killed itself
and recovery took roughly eight minutes. Restart through the CLI.

## Deploy and version discipline {#sec-ops-version}

**[ops]** Two habits, both cheap:

- **Bump the version in the same commit as the behaviour change**, never in a
  batch. The running process reports its own version at boot.
- **Keep a deploy log** of what was deployed and when. Combined with the boot
  notification's version line, it answers "is the fix live?" without anyone having
  to remember.

Commit messages carry the unit of work they belong to, which is what makes
`git log --grep` useful and what the [Engineering Log](../engineering-log.qmd) is
written from.

## The book is a build artifact too {#sec-ops-book}

This book follows the same discipline as the code, which is why it can be trusted
as documentation:

- **One command to rebuild.** `quarto render doc` from the repository root, using
  only the local Quarto CLI. No other tool, no network, no package install.
- **One command to check.** `python3 -m unittest discover tests -k book` verifies
  that every page exists, that every internal link resolves, that every page is
  well-formed, that the diagrams really are inline SVG in the output, and that no
  forbidden content has crept into either the sources or the rendered pages.
- **A sanitization gate that cannot be skipped.** The check runs over both the
  `.qmd` sources and the rendered `.html`, because a book can leak through either
  one — a private path in prose, or a personal name that arrived via a metadata
  field.
- **The output is committed-ready static HTML.** Every asset is inlined; the pages
  make no network requests at all.

The rules for adding content are in `doc/README.md`. The short version: repo paths
only, no credentials, no identifiers, no names — and the gate will tell you if you
slip.
